entities.name: National Action Party
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The National Action Party (Partido Acción Nacional, PAN), established in 1939, represents a pivotal shift in Mexican political history as the first significant opposition party to the long-dominant Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI). Founded in Mexico City, it emerged in the context of post-revolutionary Mexico, a period characterized by social upheaval and the consolidation of power by the PRI. The party's founders, including Manuel Gómez Morín and a group of intellectuals, aimed to advocate for democratic principles, Christian values, and economic liberalism against the backdrop of a state that was increasingly authoritarian and centralized in its control.

Throughout its history, the PAN has played a crucial role in Mexican politics, significantly impacting national elections and governance. The party achieved its first major electoral victory in 2000 when Vicente Fox was elected president, marking the first time in 71 years that a non-PRI candidate held the presidency. This election was a watershed moment in Mexican democracy, symbolizing the decline of the PRI's hegemonic rule and inspiring a wave of reforms aimed at increasing transparency and accountability in government.

The legacy of the National Action Party extends beyond electoral politics; it has shaped the discourse around governance, civil society, and the role of institutions in Mexico. The party's efforts to promote democracy and check the power of the PRI ushered in a new political landscape, influencing subsequent generations of political leaders and parties. Moreover, the PAN's commitment to social conservatism and market-oriented policies has left a lasting imprint on Mexican society, fueling ongoing debates about the direction of the country in the twenty-first century.
